human_interpretation_en.heading: The map starts with how you live
human_interpretation_en.text: The seven-stage map does not begin with special inner experiences. It begins with ordinary conduct: what you do with your body and speech, how you earn a living, where you choose to go, what you let your eyes linger on, and how you use food, clothing, shelter and medicine. The source's own reason is practical, not moralistic: clean conduct leaves no regret, a mind without regret becomes glad, gladness becomes joy, joy becomes calm, and calm makes steady attention possible. Only then does deeper seeing begin. In plain terms: you cannot sit still with a clear head if you are carrying things you are ashamed of.

human_interpretation_en.heading: The quiet arithmetic of honest living
human_interpretation_en.text: A remarkable share of this part is a field guide to the small, socially acceptable ways people extract things from others: false modesty that invites more generous gifts, flattery, hints dropped near the right person, talk that is mostly untrue with a little truth mixed in 'like half-cooked beans', running down someone who did not give, passing a gift from one house to another to get a bigger one back. Anyone who depends on other people's goodwill, a trader, a fundraiser, a performer, would recognise these moves. The teaching treats refusing them not as politeness but as part of the foundation of a clear mind.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Using things for what they are for
human_interpretation_en.text: Clothing is for cold, heat, insects and modesty; food is to keep the body going, taken 'like medicine by a sick person', not for fun, pride or looks; stop a few mouthfuls short and drink water. The source adds a striking frame about owing: to use what others have given without paying attention to why you are using it is to live 'on debt'; the fully free person uses things as an owner, because nothing compels them. The underlying idea is that attention at the moment of use breaks the automatic pull of wanting more.

human_interpretation_en.heading: When the good feeling is the trap
human_interpretation_en.text: The Margaya's account of the later stages contains a warning that travels well: just when practice is going well, light, joy, ease, confidence and sharpness appear, and the untrained person decides they have arrived and stops. The real problem is not the experiences but the quiet delight in them. Knowing the way from the not-way means seeing that even a breakthrough is passing and not to be held.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Integrity is a pattern, not a vow
human_interpretation_en.text: The text judges good conduct the way you would judge a length of cloth. A tear at the edge, a hole in the middle, a run of damage, a scatter of spots: each spoils it differently. It is also spoiled by what sits behind it. Keeping to a standard so that people will praise you, or to earn a reward later, already stains it, and so do the quieter indulgences that never become an outright breach. The remedy is ordinary and repeatable: mend what can be mended, drop the small habits that erode the commitment, and take it up again. The text ends with laypeople who keep their precepts by retaking them again and again. It treats this as the floor that everything else stands on, not as the goal.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Looking closely until the 'someone' dissolves into working parts
human_interpretation_en.text: The next stages ask a person to look at their own body and experience so patiently that they see only processes that depend on each other: hardness, warmth, movement, contact, feeling, knowing. The comparisons are homely. A cart is just parts put together. A house is timber, vine, clay and thatch around empty space. A drum and its sound are not mixed together. A blind man carries a lame man who gives the directions. The text's point is not that nothing matters. It is that once you see the parts working, you stop being sure there is a fixed owner inside running the show, and you no longer need to believe either that this owner lasts forever or that it is simply wiped out.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Doubt ends by tracing causes, not by choosing a comforting answer
human_interpretation_en.text: Anxious questions like 'Was I someone before? What will I become?' are not answered by faith in chance or in a maker. They are answered by following causes, the way a good doctor looks for the source of an illness or a stranger searches for a lost child's parents. Nothing is handed on whole from one life to the next. Yet what comes after really does depend on what came before, as a student recites what the teacher said without the teacher's mouth moving, or as one lamp lights another without the flame travelling. Someone who has seen this clearly is described as steadied, even though they are not yet at the end of the road.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Clarity comes from repetition, not from a single insight
human_interpretation_en.text: The text keeps returning to patient, repeated effort. Wipe the dirty mirror again. Sprinkle hot water on the sesame meal and press again. Stir the clearing seeds in the pot again until the mud settles. When progress stalls it does not call for a breakthrough. It calls for steadier attention, a suitable place, and not breaking the practice between sessions.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Nothing carries over
human_interpretation_en.text: The practice in this passage is patient, slow looking. A life is divided into decades, then years and seasons, then the parts of a day, and finally the six small movements of a single step. At each scale the same point holds: the body of childhood does not walk into adulthood, the body of a hungry season is not the body of a well-fed one, and the body in a good mood is gone when the bad mood comes. The text's own everyday picture is a new leaf. It opens pale red, turns deep red, then green, then yellow, and falls after about a year. No one stage passes into the next. We usually see one continuous thing. The text asks us to see a series of beginnings and endings, like a note on a stringed instrument that did not wait anywhere before it sounded and goes nowhere afterwards.

human_interpretation_en.heading: When things go well, that is the danger
human_interpretation_en.text: The most human part of this section is its warning about success. Once the practice starts to work, good things arrive: light, clarity, joy, ease, confidence, steady effort, calm. The text says these are not bad. The trouble starts when a person decides they have arrived, or quietly takes pride in how well they are doing, or simply wants the good feeling to continue. Even 'I am good at this' counts as a trap. The text tells of a respected teacher who believed for decades that he was finished. His own former student came to him, not to shame him, but because he saw the teacher would die still mistaken. One frightening moment showed the teacher the truth, and he asked for help. The skilled response to a good experience is to look at it as closely as at anything else: it came, it will pass, and it does not belong to anyone.

human_interpretation_en.heading: From alarm to even ground
human_interpretation_en.text: The later stages follow the way one outlook changes. At first the practitioner sees only things ending. Then everything that ends looks precarious, and the text insists this is a clear judgement, not panic: like a sighted person who sees three pits of burning coals at a town gate and knows what happens to anyone who falls in. Next comes the sense that there is no safe corner anywhere, then weariness, then wanting out. Wanting out is not enough. The person has to look again, carefully, like a fisherman who has grabbed a snake thinking it was a fish, and who must deal with it skilfully before he can let go. Only after that comes an even, balanced state, without fear of loss or delight in gain. The text compares it to a ship's bird that flies out to look for land and comes back to the mast if it finds none. Balance here does not mean giving up. It means being ready.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Different people, different doors
human_interpretation_en.text: The passage does not describe one road for everyone. Some people are carried mainly by trust, some by steadiness, some by understanding, and the text names the kind of person each becomes. Some progress with hardship and some with ease, some slowly and some quickly, and even the great disciples differed: one went easily and quickly all the way, while another went easily at first and with difficulty afterwards. What matters is that the practice is complete, not that everyone's temperament looks the same.

human_interpretation_en.heading: The leap and the landing are different moments
human_interpretation_en.text: The source separates three things we usually lump together as 'a breakthrough': clearing the fog, catching the first glimpse of what lies beyond, and actually standing there. Its man jumping a canal holds the rope until the last instant, lets go, lands shaking, and only then finds his footing. Its man looking for the moon needs three winds to clear three layers of cloud before he sees it. The practical point is modest and human: the moment you stop holding on is not the same as the moment you are secure. Being unsteady just after the change is part of the process, not a sign that it failed.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Realising it was never yours
human_interpretation_en.text: Nearly every simile in this section turns on one discovery: what someone has been holding as 'mine' belongs to someone else, or is not what it seemed. A farmer finds at dawn that the cattle he is driving are the king's. A mother finds that the child she snatched up is a stranger's. A man finds that his companion is not what he believed. In each case, seeing clearly is followed by fear, then the wish to be free, then letting go, then moving quickly, and finally standing somewhere safe. The text treats letting go as a response to seeing accurately, not as a sacrifice made through willpower.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Holding down, replacing, and cutting the root
human_interpretation_en.text: The source distinguishes three ways of getting rid of a harmful tendency. You can hold it down for a while, the way deep concentration keeps restlessness quiet. You can displace it moment by moment with its opposite, the way seeing that things arise answers the belief that nothing lasts beyond death. Or you can cut it at the root so it cannot come back, like felling a young tree before it has fruited. The text is candid that even a highly accomplished person can be ambushed by an old tendency, as in the story of the flying elder undone by a woman's song, if it was only held down and never uprooted. That honesty about relapse is one of its most human features.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Taking stock afterwards
human_interpretation_en.text: After each decisive change the source describes a quiet review: what happened, what it gave, what is gone, what is still there, and what was seen. The review includes an honest count of what remains. Nothing here claims that one turning point finishes the work. Three further stages follow, each needing the same patient process all over again.

does_not_transfer: Not a self-help ladder of 'seven steps to inner peace' or wellbeing. In the source the stages are forms of knowledge aimed at complete release from repeated existence (M:L177–L183; P4:L859), not at feeling better.

Conduct here is not respectability or being a 'nice person'. The source explicitly ranks conduct kept for reputation, praise or fear of public blame as lower (P4:L103, L113), and conduct kept in the belief that rule-keeping alone purifies as tied to wrong view (P4:L89).

The four-fold purity (P4:L163–L735) is written for ordained monastics: alms, robes, the monastic code, the monastic's ways of seeking requisites. It cannot be applied wholesale to lay life; the Margaya itself says lay purification of conduct is keeping the five precepts etc., and that not doing the reflective review is no obstacle for laypeople (M:L10, L18).

The list of places and families a monk should not frequent (P4:L241–L285: sex workers, widows, older unmarried women, paṇḍakas, nuns, taverns, rulers, other sects, hostile households) is protective guidance for a celibate renunciant in its original setting. It must not be carried over as a judgement on any of these groups today.

Stories of monks who let themselves be burned rather than cut a living creeper, or who broke their own thigh as a pledge to robbers (P4:L607–L613, L759–L763), should not be turned into a modern slogan of 'integrity at any cost' or presented as models of self-harm.
Reflective use of requisites is not a minimalism or frugality lifestyle brand; its purpose in the source is to cut craving and avoid being a 'debtor' to donors (P4:L711, L735).

Light, bliss and sharpness during meditation (M:L103–L121) are not the goal or proof of success; the source calls attachment to them a corruption (M:L123–L125). A 'peak experience' framing inverts the teaching.
Miracle elements in the exemplary stories (a tree deity holding a lamp, a truth-act healing a mother, P4:L642, L646–L650) are part of the source's teaching narrative, not documentary evidence.

'Just be a good person': the source's purity of conduct is built around a detailed monastic rulebook (seven classes of offence, specific rules on celibacy). The lay version exists, but only as a short closing note.

'There's no self, so no one is responsible': the source keeps action and its results fully in force (twelve kinds of action, a round of action and a round of result). It denies only a separate doer or experiencer standing behind the process.

'Life is suffering' as a mood or a worldview: the forty ways of seeing the aggregates (disease, boil, dart, murderer and so on) are contemplative lenses used to loosen attachment during training, not a verdict on how to feel about life.

'Everyone goes on to another life in the same way': the source's account of rebirth (the womb passage, beings born spontaneously, beings without perception) is doctrinal cosmology, not a claim that can be tested on camera or presented as fact.

The body counts (1,152 material units in the thirty-two parts, and so on) and the mind-moment timings belong to an analytic system for meditation. They should not be presented as biology or physiology.
'Lesser stream-enterer' is not a certificate or a status someone can be shown to hold. The text uses it for a mundane stage that can still be lost ('one who has not fallen away from' it).
The Aggikkhandhopama imagery (embracing fire, iron bands, molten iron balls) is aimed at monks who are unvirtuous yet accept offerings. It should not be recast as a general threat of punishment.

'Everything is temporary, so enjoy the moment.' The source uses impermanence to lead towards disenchantment and release. It does not use it to encourage savouring experience; relish (nikanti) is named as the subtlest trap (L1965, L2161).

'Chase peak experiences.' Light, rapture, bliss and strong confidence are listed as corruptions when they are taken as the goal (L2163–L2165). A modern framing that treats spiritual highs as proof of progress reverses the text.
The 'fear' stage is not anxiety or trauma to be dramatised. The text says this knowledge does not itself fear; it is a calm judgement (L2311–L2313).

Disenchantment is not depression or cynicism about life. The same passage says the practitioner delights in the practice itself (L2363), and among the benefits of the knowledge of dissolution it lists fearlessness, patience, gentleness and pure livelihood (L2267–L2285).

Equanimity towards formations is not indifference to people. It is a balanced stance towards arising and passing phenomena, without fear or delight (L2479–L2481). The source's simile of a man indifferent to a wife he has divorced is a period image and should not be lifted as a relationship lesson.

'Not-self' does not mean 'you don't matter' or 'no one is responsible'. The text's point is that even the sense of 'I am the one meditating' has to loosen (L1967–L1971), and it still speaks throughout of effort, method and teachers.

The body-decade scheme (a hundred years in ten decades, with 'play', 'beauty', 'strength', 'wisdom', 'decline' and so on) is a traditional contemplation device. It should not be presented as a claim about how real people age.

This is not a 'sudden enlightenment' or 'breakthrough moment' story in the self-help sense. The source places the decisive moments at the end of a long, ordered sequence of purifications and insight knowledges, and repeats the whole sequence for each of the three higher paths.

'Change of lineage' is not a personal rebrand or an identity shift. In the source it is a single mind-moment that takes the unconditioned as its object, and it explicitly cannot remove defilements by itself.
Cutting defilements off at the root is not suppression or discipline. The source classes suppression, even by deep concentration, as a lesser and reversible form of abandoning.

The four functions (understanding suffering, abandoning its origin, realising cessation, developing the path) are not a four-step plan to work through in order. The source insists that they happen together in one moment, like a lamp that burns, lights, dispels darkness and uses oil all at once.

The fear and disenchantment in the similes (the burning house, the demoness, the stolen child) are stages of clear seeing about conditioned things, not depression, burnout or advice to flee people. The similes about women should not be lifted out as statements about real relationships.

Statements such as 'at most seven more births' or 'will not return to the sense world' are doctrinal claims about rebirth. They should not be recast as motivational promises or tested against anyone's life.

story_seeds.seed: A market trader whose regular customers trust the weighing scale, over one ordinary day.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Weighing and bagging, small decisions about rounding up or down, customers who do not check the scale, credit given in a notebook, the trader's own account of why they trade the way they do.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Purity of livelihood is the ground floor of the whole map; the source spends many pages on the small, tempting ways of getting more than is fair. The link is honest but indirect: the trader is not a monastic and the four-fold purity is monastic.
story_seeds.setting_type: Weekly village fair or town fish/vegetable market
story_seeds.risk: Turning one person into a morality exhibit, or implying that other traders cheat. Needs the trader's full consent and must avoid any hidden-camera 'test' of honesty.

story_seeds.seed: Young novices on a dawn alms round and at the meal that follows.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Walking in line with lowered eyes, households waiting with rice and curries, the moment of receiving, and, if the community does this, a spoken reflection before eating; what is left in the bowl.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Directly touches sense restraint, pure seeking of requisites and reflective use of food, all described at length in this part (P4:L311–L315, L541–L551).
story_seeds.setting_type: Village temple with a resident community of novices
story_seeds.risk: Exoticising monastic life or staging an alms round for the camera. Requires the temple's permission and should follow its actual routine; do not assume a pre-meal recitation exists without checking.

story_seeds.seed: A family preparing a household almsgiving from the night before.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Cooking through the night, relatives arriving, arranging the food, the offering, the monks eating, the family eating afterwards, conversations about why they give.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source examines the giver-receiver relationship closely: donors' faith, the danger of receivers manipulating donors, and the idea that careless use of a gift is living 'on debt' (P4:L387–L391, L709–L735).
story_seeds.risk: Implying judgement of the monks who receive, or turning a family's devotion into an illustration. The film must stand as a family story first.

story_seeds.seed: Lay people beginning a multi-day silent meditation retreat.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Formally taking precepts on arrival, handing in phones, the timetable, meals in silence, first-day restlessness, and participants' own words at the end about what surprised them.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Shows conduct being set up as the ground for concentration (M:L46; P4:L821–L835), and could leave room for the Margaya's warning about mistaking a good experience for arrival (M:L125), in participants' own words.
story_seeds.setting_type: Forest or hillside meditation centre that accepts lay retreatants
story_seeds.risk: Inner states cannot be filmed; the camera intrudes on silence. Filming must follow the centre's rules and never pressure participants to describe experiences or claim attainments.

story_seeds.seed: Lay devotees who take the eight precepts on a full-moon day, keep them through the day and night, and take them again the next month
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The formal request for the precepts at dawn, white clothes, the long day of restraint (no afternoon meal, quiet hours), small lapses and self-corrections, the same people returning at the next full moon
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source closes the first purification by telling laypeople to keep their own precepts and retake them again and again [C097-P4:L1022]. Conduct appears as something repeated and repaired, not declared once.
story_seeds.setting_type: A village temple or a meditation hall on a full-moon day
story_seeds.risk: It could become a pious display or a before-and-after morality tale. Filming people while they practise needs clear consent and must not disturb them.

story_seeds.seed: A household or small community that still clears muddy well or tank water by rubbing clearing-nut seeds inside a clay pot
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Hands rubbing the seed on the inner wall of the pot, the water clouding and then slowly settling over time, the same work repeated when the first attempt does not clear it
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source compares persistent attention to matter with stirring clearing-nut seeds again and again until the mud sinks and the water becomes clear [C097-P4:L1156–L1162].
story_seeds.setting_type: A rural home in a dry-zone village with a well or a small tank
story_seeds.risk: The practice may now be rare. It must not be revived or staged for the film. Scarce water and poverty should not be made picturesque.

story_seeds.seed: A traditional oil mill where sesame is pressed, wetted with hot water and pressed again before the oil comes
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Seed being ground, water sprinkled on, repeated turns of the press, the moment the first oil appears, the miller judging when to add more water
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's image of not throwing away the sesame meal when one or two pressings yield nothing, but sprinkling hot water and pressing again [C097-P4:L1154].
story_seeds.setting_type: A small rural oil mill or a family-run pressing operation
story_seeds.risk: It could become a craft-nostalgia piece in which the doctrine is bolted on. Draught-animal welfare, if an animal-driven press is used, must not be glossed over.

story_seeds.seed: A rural veterinary officer or traditional healer working patiently back from symptoms to causes before treating
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Questions to the owner or patient about food, water, weather and recent changes, examination, eliminating possibilities, and explaining the likely cause instead of blaming bad luck
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source opens the purification by overcoming doubt with a skilled doctor seeking a disease's origin, and insists that things arise neither without cause nor from a creator, but from specific conditions [C097-P4:L1252–L1260].
story_seeds.setting_type: A farming area served by a veterinary office or a village clinic
story_seeds.risk: Medical privacy and consent. The film must not appear to endorse any particular treatment, or cast the practitioner as a mouthpiece for doctrine.

story_seeds.seed: A temple gardener or nursery keeper who tends young trees through a full year and watches individual shoots change colour, harden and drop.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The same branch filmed at intervals: a pale red new shoot, deeper red, soft green, dark green, yellowing, the leaf falling and being swept up. The gardener's daily round, watering, pruning, and how they talk about particular trees.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's own example of outside, non-living-body matter is a young tree shoot. It moves from pale red to green to yellow and falls, and no stage passes into the next (L1919–L1925). The film is about care and time; the leaf carries the idea without anyone explaining it.
story_seeds.setting_type: A temple garden, village home garden or small plant nursery in Sri Lanka.
story_seeds.risk: Time-lapse leaf footage can easily become a screensaver metaphor. The gardener's own relationship with the trees has to carry the film, and the leaf should never be narrated as a doctrine.

story_seeds.seed: A master of a traditional craft, such as drumming, mask carving or dance, gently correcting an apprentice who has just had a good day and thinks they have mastered it.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Repeated practice sessions, the apprentice's visible pleasure after a breakthrough, the teacher's restraint or correction, and the next session, where the 'mastery' slips and the work continues.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The ten corruptions of insight describe exactly this moment. Genuine progress (clarity, confidence, energy, joy) turns into a trap when it is taken as arrival or as a reason for pride (L2163–L2171). The teacher-and-student story in the source shows the correction as an act of care (L2133–L2137).
story_seeds.setting_type: A traditional arts workshop, village dance school or craft household in Sri Lanka.
story_seeds.risk: The apprentice must not be humiliated for the camera, and the correction must not be staged. Film only the teaching that actually happens, with both parties' consent, and do not script a 'lesson'.

story_seeds.seed: An inland fisher at a reservoir who sometimes finds a water snake in a trap or net and has to deal with it calmly before going on.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Traps set and hauled; the moment of recognition when a catch turns out not to be a fish; the practised, unhurried handling and release; and the fisher's own account of how they learned not to panic.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's image for the stages from alarm to re-examination to release is a man who reaches into a fish trap, grabs a snake thinking it is a fish, sees the markings, and frees himself with skill instead of flailing (L2387–L2403).
story_seeds.setting_type: A village tank or inland reservoir with traditional trap or net fishing.
story_seeds.risk: Sensationalising snakes, or putting fisher or animal at risk for a shot. The camera should never wait for or provoke an encounter. If one does not happen naturally, the fisher's account is enough.

story_seeds.seed: A lay or monastic meditation teacher's regular one-to-one check-ins with students on a long retreat, where the teacher asks about experiences and responds to reports of light, joy or 'breakthroughs'.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: With full consent and only where the teacher allows it: the rhythm of the retreat day, walking meditation, the brief interview format, and the teacher's steady, unexcited response to reports of unusual experiences.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source describes the practitioner's discernment of 'this is path, this is not path' as a purification in its own right (L2173–L2177), and it frames that discernment through a teacher who comes to help (L2137).
story_seeds.setting_type: A forest hermitage or meditation centre in Sri Lanka that runs structured retreats.
story_seeds.risk: Filming private inner states is intrusive, and a camera would change the retreat. The film could slide into lecture or into selling a spiritual product. Treat this seed as possible only if the institution and the individuals clearly want it, and prefer reflective interviews after the retreat to footage recorded during it.

story_seeds.seed: Villagers crossing a flooded irrigation channel or stream by rope, log or pole in the monsoon season, where the crossing is a daily necessity
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The run-up, the grip on the rope, the moment of letting go, the unsteady landing and the first sure step on the far bank, repeated by different people with different levels of confidence
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It mirrors the source's own canal-jump simile for conformity, change-of-lineage and path: holding on, releasing, landing unsteadily, then standing firm. The film would be about the crossing and never needs to explain the doctrine.
story_seeds.setting_type: Rural wet-zone or intermediate-zone village with seasonal streams or irrigation channels
story_seeds.risk: Asking people to cross for the camera, or making a crossing look more dangerous than it is, would be staging. Film only crossings people already make, and do not encourage risk.

story_seeds.seed: Dawn in a dry-zone herding community after cattle have broken out overnight, as owners track, sort and return animals that are not theirs
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Hoof tracks at first light, herders reading brands and markings, the moment someone realises an animal belongs to a neighbour, and animals being handed back or driven home
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's cattle simile turns on recognising at dawn that what you took as yours is not. A real, low-stakes version of that recognition, followed by letting go, happens in ordinary herding life.
story_seeds.setting_type: Dry-zone village with free-grazing cattle and shared pasture or tank bed
story_seeds.risk: Disputes over animals can carry real tension or legal weight. Do not film conflicts or frame anyone as a thief. Stick to routine sorting and ask consent.

story_seeds.seed: A person whose daily task is lighting and tending oil lamps, at a village shrine or in a household that keeps lamps every evening
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Trimming wicks, pouring oil, the flame catching, darkness pulling back from the walls, and the oil level falling through the night until morning
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source uses one lamp doing four things at once (burning the wick, dispelling darkness, spreading light, using up oil) for the four simultaneous functions of path knowledge. The lamp-keeper's routine shows that simultaneity without any explanation.
story_seeds.setting_type: Village temple or devāla lamp house, or a rural home that keeps evening lamps
story_seeds.risk: It could become a pretty metaphor with no human stake. The film must be about the keeper's life, duty and continuity, not only about the flame.

story_seeds.seed: Night fishers or others whose work depends on reading the moon and sky, waiting for cloud to clear before deciding to go out
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Watching the sky, clouds thinning in stages, the moon appearing, and the decision being made and acted on
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It echoes the moon-behind-three-layers-of-cloud simile: three winds clear thick, middle and thin cloud before the moon can be seen. The waiting and the clearing are real and consequential for their work.
story_seeds.risk: The weather cannot be scheduled, so it would be tempting to fake the sequence in the edit. Be honest about the timeline, and avoid romanticising dangerous conditions.

cross_source_notes: Scope: the Pradeepika part 1 (P4:L1–860) covers only purification of conduct, in great depth; the Margaya covers all seven purifications in 185 lines, with only one paragraph-level section on conduct (M:L6–L18). For the later six purifications in this part, the Margaya is the only source read; the Pradeepika's treatment of them lies in parts 2–4.

Both define the monastic purification of conduct as the four-fold purity (P4:L26, L163–L171; M:L10). The Margaya adds an explicit lay version (five precepts etc.; lay livelihood = avoiding killing and the five wrong trades; M:L10, L16); the Pradeepika's material is monastic, mentioning lay conduct only as a classification (P4:L149).

Sense restraint: the Margaya equates it with mindfulness itself (M:L14); the Pradeepika defines it as restraining the six faculties (P4:L325) and says it is perfected by mindfulness (P4:L593, L617), locating restraint or its absence in the javana moments of the cognitive process (P4:L335–L349).

Reflective use of requisites: the Margaya identifies it with the reflecting knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that prevents confusion, craving and intoxication (M:L18); the Pradeepika defines it as use of the four requisites after reflection (P4:L529) and says it is perfected by wisdom (P4:L597). Complementary, not contradictory.

The Pradeepika pairs each of the four with a faculty (faith, mindfulness, effort, wisdom; P4:L589–L597) and a kind of purity (confession, resolve, seeking, reviewing; P4:L717–L727). The Margaya has neither pairing.

The Margaya's count of insight knowledges: ten from comprehension (sammasana) to conformity (anuloma), of which nine (rise-and-fall to conformity) constitute purification by knowledge of the way (M:L132–L136). The Pradeepika's scope note likewise names 'විදර්ශනා ඥාන නවය' for this purification (P4:L13), so the two agree on nine; the Pradeepika's detailed treatment is outside this part.

The Pradeepika's scope note says its maggāmagga section contains sammasana, the eighteen great insights and the ten corruptions (P4:L13). The Margaya mentions tilakkhaṇa, the three contemplations and the ten corruptions, but not the eighteen great insights (M:L74–L125). Items 18–35 of the Pradeepika's abandonment table (P4:L791–L813) are these eighteen contemplations, listed here under conduct.
